title: Dependency and Package Security
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terminology of Dependency and Package Security.
Apply dependency and package security to a small synthetic example and identify evidence that supports the conclusion.
Identify a relevant limitation or failure mode and describe a safe defensive response.

content.intro: This lesson covers dependency and package security in the DevSecOps and Software Supply Chain Security track. It preserves the PDF's listed subtopics and develops a small, checkable defensive example. You will practice stating scope and assumptions, selecting relevant evidence, and describing what remains uncertain.
content.why_it_matters: Protect pipeline identities and artifacts, pin and review dependencies, keep secrets out of logs, and require human approval for high-impact changes. The specific focus here is dependency and package security; connect each subtopic to an observable check or a documented decision.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Dependency and Package Security focuses on direct and transitive dependencies; dependency lockfiles; vulnerable package detection. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case.

items.title: Direct and Transitive Dependencies
items.text: For direct and transitive dependencies, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: Dependency Lockfiles
items.text: Cloud and delivery security combine least-privilege identities, hardened defaults, approved dependencies, secret management, artifact provenance, logging, and repeatable deployment checks. Verify service-specific behavior and avoid placing secrets in source or logs.

items.title: Vulnerable Package Detection
items.text: A vulnerability is a weakness that could be used or triggered to cause harm. Validate its existence safely, record affected versions and preconditions, and prioritize using exposure, impact, threat context, and available mitigations.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification
content_blocks.text: DevSecOps makes security verifiable throughout build, review, release, deployment, and maintenance instead of leaving it until the end. Before attempting any live security test, obtain explicit permission and verify that the target and method are within scope. When a secure isolated runner is not available, treat the code as a local/synthetic example and do not run arbitrary content on production infrastructure.

content_blocks.title: Run, verify, and reset
content_blocks.text: Review the python snippet as a local calculation. If you choose to run this example, use Python 3 and synthetic inputs in a disposable local environment; compare the displayed expected output with what you observe. If the result differs, check the copied inputs and runtime version, restore the synthetic input, and repeat. No scan, external request, or production change is needed.

content_blocks.text: Recap: Dependency and Package Security focuses on direct and transitive dependencies; dependency lockfiles; vulnerable package detection. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case. Apply this to one controlled example, record evidence, and note an important edge case. Next, continue to the next lesson or revisit the prerequisite concept if a key term is unclear.

content.task: Create a concise, reviewable artifact demonstrating Dependency and Package Security. Use synthetic data or a controlled local training environment only. Include the relevant syllabus subtopics (Direct and Transitive Dependencies; Dependency Lockfiles; Vulnerable Package Detection), state assumptions, show what evidence would support your conclusion, identify one failure mode, and recommend a defensive next step. Do not test systems outside written authorization.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use only a synthetic dataset, a disposable local lab, or an explicitly authorized system.
Include a clear scope/assumption statement and enough sanitized evidence for another learner to follow the reasoning.
Explain one limitation, edge case, or failure mode.
Recommend a proportionate defensive control and describe how to verify it safely.
hints: Write the expected behavior and test boundary before looking at a result.
Change one assumption at a time; compare results against the original synthetic case.
Record evidence and uncertainty separately, and select a proportionate protective action.

If an output differs, check the input and runtime version; do not broaden the activity to an unrelated system.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one observation as conclusive proof.
common_mistakes.why: Security telemetry and tests cover only the cases they were designed to observe.
common_mistakes.fix: Corroborate important claims and document coverage gaps.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing a target without confirming authorization.
common_mistakes.why: A technical ability to reach a system does not grant permission to assess it.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic input or a local lab; stop if the approved scope is unclear.

common_mistakes.problem: Skipping the version and context assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Security controls and protocol details vary across implementations and deployment models.
common_mistakes.fix: Record versions, configuration, expected output, and the source used for verification.

summary: Dependency and Package Security is best understood within its defined scope and trust boundaries.
Use relevant evidence and test both an expected case and a meaningful failure case.
Record uncertainty and choose a proportionate, authorized defensive next step.
